topics.title: 3.1.1 Section A: The challenge of natural hazards

outcomes.text: Define a natural hazard and list the types of natural hazard.
Explain the factors that affect hazard risk.
Explain why natural hazards pose major risks to people and property.
Explain plate tectonics theory.
Describe the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes and its link to plate margins.
Explain the processes at constructive, destructive and conservative margins that cause earthquakes and eruptions.
Distinguish primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses to a tectonic hazard.
Use two named examples to show how effects and responses differ between richer and poorer areas.
Explain why people continue to live in areas at risk from tectonic hazards.
Explain how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce tectonic risks.
Describe the general atmospheric circulation model with pressure belts and surface winds.
Describe the global distribution of tropical storms and its link to atmospheric circulation.
Explain the causes and sequence of formation of tropical storms and their structure.
Explain how climate change might affect storm distribution, frequency and intensity.
Distinguish primary and secondary effects and immediate and long-term responses to tropical storms, using a named example.
Explain how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce storm effects.
Give an overview of the weather hazards experienced in the UK.
Use a recent UK extreme weather event to show its causes, impacts and management strategies.
Describe evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme.

subtopics.title: Evidence and causes of climate change

outcomes.text: Describe evidence for climate change from the Quaternary to the present.
Explain natural causes (orbital changes, volcanic activity, solar output) and human causes (fossil fuels, agriculture, deforestation).
Give an overview of the effects of climate change on people and the environment.
Explain mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, tree planting and international agreements.
Explain adaptation: changing agriculture, managing water supply and reducing sea-level risk.
Use a small-scale UK ecosystem to explain producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling.
Explain the balance between ecosystem components and the effect of changing one.
Give an overview of the distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems.
Describe the physical characteristics of a tropical rainforest.
Explain the interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Explain how plants and animals adapt to rainforest conditions and the issues of biodiversity.
Describe changing rates of deforestation.
Using a rainforest case study, explain the causes of deforestation.
Using the case study, explain the impacts: economic development, soil erosion and climate change.
Explain the value of tropical rainforests to people and the environment.
Explain strategies: selective logging, replanting, conservation, education, ecotourism, hardwood agreements and debt reduction.
Describe the physical characteristics of a hot desert.
Explain the interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people, and adaptations.
Explain the issues of desert biodiversity.
Using a case study, explain opportunities: minerals, energy, farming and tourism.
Explain the challenges: extreme temperatures, water supply and inaccessibility.
Explain the causes of desertification on desert fringes.
Explain strategies to reduce desertification: water and soil management, tree planting and appropriate technology.
Describe the physical characteristics of polar and tundra environments.
Explain the interdependence of climate, permafrost, soils, plants, animals and people, and adaptations.
Explain the issues of cold environment biodiversity.
Using a case study, explain opportunities: minerals, energy, fishing and tourism.
Explain the challenges: extreme temperature, inaccessibility, buildings and infrastructure.
Explain the value of cold environments as wilderness and why they should be protected.
Explain how technology, governments, agreements and conservation groups balance development and conservation.

topics.title: 3.1.3 Section C: Physical landscapes in the UK

outcomes.text: Give an overview of the location of major UK upland and lowland areas and river systems.
Explain why the UK has diverse landscapes.
Describe wave types and characteristics.
Explain coastal weathering (mechanical, chemical) and mass movement (sliding, slumping, rock falls).
Explain erosion (hydraulic power, abrasion, attrition), longshore drift transportation and why deposition occurs.
Explain how geology and rock type influence coastal forms.
Describe how headlands and bays, cliffs and wave cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks form.
Describe how beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars form.
Use a UK coastline example to identify landforms of erosion and deposition.
Explain the costs and benefits of hard engineering: sea walls, rock armour, gabions and groynes.
Explain soft engineering (beach nourishment, dune regeneration) and managed retreat.
Use a UK coastal scheme to show reasons, strategy, effects and conflicts.
Describe a river's long profile and changing valley cross profile.
Explain erosion, transportation (traction, saltation, suspension, solution) and why rivers deposit sediment.
Describe how interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges form.
Describe how meanders and ox-bow lakes form.
Describe how levees, flood plains and estuaries form.
Use a UK river valley example to identify landforms of erosion and deposition.
Explain how precipitation, geology, relief and land use affect flood risk.
Use hydrographs to show the relationship between precipitation and discharge.
Explain the costs and benefits of hard engineering: dams, straightening, embankments and relief channels.
Explain soft engineering: warnings, flood plain zoning, tree planting and river restoration.
Use a UK flood scheme to show why it was needed, the strategy and social, economic and environmental issues.
Describe the maximum extent of UK ice cover in the last ice age.
Explain freeze-thaw, abrasion, plucking, rotational slip, bulldozing and glacial deposition of till and outwash.
Describe how corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, troughs, ribbon lakes and hanging valleys form.
Describe how erratics, drumlins and moraines form.
Use a UK upland example to identify glacial landforms.
Give an overview of tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying in glaciated uplands.
Explain land use conflicts and conflicts between development and conservation.
Use a UK glaciated tourist area to show attractions, impacts and management.

topics.title: 3.2.1 Section A: Urban issues and challenges

outcomes.text: Describe the global pattern of urban change and urban trends in HICs and LICs.
Explain how migration (push-pull) and natural increase affect the rate of urbanisation.
Describe the emergence of megacities.
Using a case study, describe the city's location and importance regionally, nationally and internationally.
Explain the causes of growth: natural increase and migration.
Explain social opportunities from urban growth: services, water and energy.
Explain how urban industrial areas stimulate economic development.
Explain challenges of slums and squatter settlements, and of clean water, sanitation and energy.
Explain challenges of services, unemployment, crime, waste, pollution and congestion.
Use an example of urban planning that improves life for the urban poor.
Give an overview of UK population distribution and major cities.
Using a UK city case study, describe its location and importance and the effects of migration on its character.
Explain opportunities: cultural mix, recreation, employment, integrated transport and urban greening.
Explain challenges: deprivation, inequality, dereliction, brownfield and greenfield building, and waste.
Explain urban sprawl, rural-urban fringe change and commuter settlements.
Use a regeneration project to show why the area needed it and the project's main features.
Describe sustainable urban living: water and energy conservation, recycling and green space.
Explain how transport strategies reduce traffic congestion.

topics.title: 3.2.2 Section B: The changing economic world

outcomes.text: Classify parts of the world by economic development and quality of life.
Use measures such as GNI per head, birth and death rates, infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy, safe water and the HDI.
Explain the limitations of development measures.
Link the stages of the Demographic Transition Model to level of development.
Explain physical, economic and historical causes of uneven development.
Explain consequences: disparities in wealth and health, and international migration.
Give an overview of strategies: investment, industry and tourism, aid, intermediate technology, fairtrade, debt relief and microfinance.
Use an example of tourism growth in an LIC or NEE reducing the development gap.
Using a case study of an LIC or NEE, describe its location, importance and political, social, cultural and environmental context.
Explain its changing industrial structure and how manufacturing stimulates development.
Explain the role of transnational corporations and their advantages and disadvantages to the host country.
Explain changing political and trading relationships and the types and impacts of international aid.
Explain environmental impacts of development and effects on quality of life.
Explain causes of UK economic change: de-industrialisation, globalisation and government policy.
Describe the move to a post-industrial economy: IT, services, finance, research and business parks.
Explain industry's impact on the environment and an example of more sustainable industrial development.
Explain social and economic change in rural areas of population growth and decline.
Describe improvements in road, rail, port and airport capacity.
Explain the north-south divide and strategies to reduce regional differences.
Describe the UK's links through trade, culture, transport and communication, and with the EU and Commonwealth.

topics.title: 3.2.3 Section C: The challenge of resource management

outcomes.text: Explain the significance of food, water and energy to economic and social well-being.
Give an overview of global inequalities in the supply and consumption of resources.
Give an overview of resources in the UK.
Explain UK food trends: high-value imports, year-round demand, food miles, local sourcing and agribusiness.
Explain UK water trends: changing demand, quality, pollution, deficit and surplus areas and transfers.
Explain UK energy trends: changing energy mix, falling domestic fossil fuel supply and economic and environmental issues.
Describe global patterns of calorie intake and food supply.
Explain why food consumption is rising and the factors affecting food supply.
Explain impacts of food insecurity: famine, undernutrition, soil erosion, rising prices and unrest.
Describe strategies: irrigation, aeroponics, hydroponics, new green revolution, biotechnology and appropriate technology.
Use a large-scale agricultural development to show advantages and disadvantages.
Describe sustainable food supplies: organic farming, permaculture, urban farming, sustainable fish and meat, seasonal food and less waste.
Use a local scheme in an LIC or NEE to increase sustainable food.
Describe global patterns of water surplus and deficit.
Explain why water consumption is rising and what affects water availability.
Explain impacts of water insecurity: disease, pollution, food and industrial output, and conflict.
Describe strategies: diversion, storage, dams, reservoirs, water transfers and desalination.
Use a large-scale water transfer scheme to show advantages and disadvantages.
Describe water conservation, groundwater management, recycling and grey water.
Use a local scheme in an LIC or NEE to increase sustainable water.
Describe global distribution of energy consumption and supply.
Explain why energy consumption is rising and the factors affecting energy supply.
Explain impacts of energy insecurity: sensitive-area exploration, costs, food and industrial output, and conflict.
Compare renewable (biomass, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, wave, solar) and non-renewable (fossil fuels, nuclear) sources.
Use a fossil fuel extraction example to show advantages and disadvantages.
Explain individual energy use, carbon footprints and energy conservation in homes, workplaces and transport.
Use a local renewable energy scheme in an LIC or NEE.
Analyse a geographical issue at several scales, drawing on more than one theme from the physical and human units.
Weigh stakeholders' views and advantages and disadvantages, then justify a chosen option.
Choose a suitable enquiry question and the theory behind it, with sources, locations and risk management.
Distinguish primary from secondary data, and measure and record data using sampling methods.
Select and use presentation methods, then describe, analyse and explain results with statistics and anomalies.
Draw conclusions linked to the aims and evaluate data collection, limitations and reliability.
Use latitude and longitude, and describe patterns on atlas and thematic maps.
Read OS maps at 1:50 000 and 1:25 000 with four- and six-figure grid references.
Use scale, distance, direction, gradient, contours and spot heights, and draw cross sections.
Infer physical landscape and human activity from map evidence.
Use and interpret ground, aerial and satellite photographs, sketch maps and annotated diagrams.
Select and construct line, bar, pie, histogram, divided bar, scatter graphs and population pyramids.
Complete and interpret choropleth, isoline, dot, desire line, proportional symbol and flow line maps.
Understand number, area, scale, proportion, ratio, magnitude and frequency.
Design data collection sheets with attention to accuracy, sample size and reliability.
Calculate mean, median, mode, range, quartiles and interquartile range.
Calculate percentage change, describe bivariate data with trend lines, and spot weak statistical presentation.
Use qualitative and quantitative primary and secondary data, including maps, GIS and satellite imagery.
Pose enquiry questions and build well-evidenced extended written arguments.
Communicate information for different audiences with good literacy.
